docs.title: The world in numbers, late 2026: five signals from the newest World Bank data
docs.text: The World Bank updated its World Development Indicators on 11 November 2026. Working from the same 15 indicators as this site's dashboard, five signals stand out: steady growth, a more connected world, wider financial inclusion, slow poverty progress — and one series that has quietly stopped in 2023.

docs.title: The world in numbers, late 2026: five signals from the newest World Bank data
docs.text: Every few months, quietly, the world's most-used development dataset changes. On 11 November 2026 the World Bank published its latest World Development Indicators update, adding 2025 values for many headline series. I track 15 of those indicators on this site's dashboard, across 32 countries and economies, and I re-check them every week. Here is what the newest vintage says. All figures below are world aggregates from that update. One caution before the numbers: each indicator keeps its own calendar. Some series already reach 2025, others stop in 2024 because they rest on household surveys, and one, as we will see, has not moved since 2023. The latest year is part of the story.

docs.title: The world in numbers, late 2026: five signals from the newest World Bank data — Growth held steady
docs.text: Growth held steady The world economy grew 2.92% in 2025 , and GDP per capita reached $14,406 . Inflation eased to 3.04% , exports held at 29.5% of GDP , and unemployment sat at 4.79% . None of these numbers describes a boom, but together they describe an expansion that is still intact: output rising, price pressures cooling, and labour markets holding. For programme teams, this is the backdrop against which country-level results should be read — a country growing more slowly than 2.9% in 2025 was losing ground against the world average.

docs.title: The world in numbers, late 2026: five signals from the newest World Bank data — A more connected world
docs.text: A more connected world 73.6% of the world's people used the internet in 2025 — roughly three in four. Access to electricity reached 91.9% in 2024 , its latest year. Connectivity is no longer a niche concern for digital programmes; it is close to a default condition in most places where development teams work. The remaining gaps are increasingly concentrated: the roughly 8% of people still without electricity, and the quarter of the world not yet online, are the hardest to reach, and averages will flatter any programme that does not look for them specifically.

docs.title: The world in numbers, late 2026: five signals from the newest World Bank data — Financial inclusion kept climbing
docs.text: Financial inclusion kept climbing 78.7% of adults worldwide owned an account in 2024 , the latest Global Findex reading. As covered in my earlier article on the Findex 2025, the recent story is not just access but use — saving, payments and resilience. Two practical notes for analysts: this series is survey-based, so it appears only in survey years (2011, 2014, 2017, 2021, 2024), and a dashboard that seems to show "no change" between those years is showing the survey calendar, not stagnation.

docs.title: The world in numbers, late 2026: five signals from the newest World Bank data — Poverty is moving slowly
docs.text: Poverty is moving slowly The share of people living in extreme poverty was 10.1% in 2024 , the latest available year. Life expectancy reached 73.5 years in 2024 , and world population passed 8.22 billion in 2025 . Poverty estimates rest on household surveys that take time to collect and process, so the world learns its poverty rate roughly two years late. Decisions made this year are therefore being taken with a poverty picture from 2024 — worth remembering whenever a single headline figure is asked to carry more weight than it can bear.

docs.title: The world in numbers, late 2026: five signals from the newest World Bank data — The signal in the gaps
docs.text: The signal in the gaps The most useful finding in this update may be an absence. The world cereal yield series — a basic food-security indicator — still ends in 2023, at 4,229 kg per hectare , even after the November 2026 update. Agriculture was 4.01% of world GDP in 2025 and still employs 25.8% of workers , yet one of its simplest productivity measures is running three years behind. Dashboards rarely announce a stale series; the chart simply stops, or worse, quietly repeats. The habit that protects you is unglamorous: check the latest year of every indicator you publish, every time you publish. It is why the 15 indicators behind this site's dashboard get re-verified weekly, and why the dashboard

docs.title: Le monde en chiffres, fin 2026 : cinq signaux des nouvelles données de la Banque mondiale
docs.text: La Banque mondiale a mis à jour ses Indicateurs du développement dans le monde le 11 novembre 2026. À partir des 15 indicateurs du tableau de bord de ce site, cinq signaux ressortent : une croissance stable, un monde plus connecté, une inclusion financière élargie, une pauvreté qui recule lentement — et une série discrètement figée en 2023.

docs.title: Le monde en chiffres, fin 2026 : cinq signaux des nouvelles données de la Banque mondiale
docs.text: Tous les quelques mois, discrètement, le jeu de données sur le développement le plus utilisé au monde change. Le 11 novembre 2026, la Banque mondiale a publié la dernière mise à jour de ses Indicateurs du développement dans le monde, avec des valeurs 2025 pour plusieurs grandes séries. Je suis 15 de ces indicateurs dans le tableau de bord de ce site, pour 32 pays et économies, et je les revérifie chaque semaine. Voici ce que dit la cuvée la plus récente. Tous les chiffres ci-dessous sont des agrégats mondiaux tirés de cette mise à jour. Une précaution avant les chiffres : chaque indicateur suit son propre calendrier. Certaines séries atteignent déjà 2025, d'autres s'arrêtent en 2024 parce qu'elles reposent sur

docs.title: Le monde en chiffres, fin 2026 : cinq signaux des nouvelles données de la Banque mondiale
docs.text: des enquêtes auprès des ménages, et l'une d'elles, nous le verrons, n'a pas bougé depuis 2023. L'année la plus récente fait partie de l'histoire.

docs.title: Le monde en chiffres, fin 2026 : cinq signaux des nouvelles données de la Banque mondiale — Une croissance stable
docs.text: Une croissance stable L'économie mondiale a crû de 2,92 % en 2025 , et le PIB par habitant a atteint 14 406 $ . L'inflation a reculé à 3,04 % , les exportations se sont maintenues à 29,5 % du PIB et le chômage s'établissait à 4,79 % . Aucun de ces chiffres ne décrit un boom, mais ensemble ils décrivent une expansion toujours intacte : une production en hausse, des tensions sur les prix qui s'apaisent et des marchés du travail qui tiennent. Pour les équipes de programmes, c'est l'arrière-plan auquel comparer les résultats par pays : un pays dont la croissance était inférieure à 2,9 % en 2025 perdait du terrain par rapport à la moyenne mondiale.

docs.title: Le monde en chiffres, fin 2026 : cinq signaux des nouvelles données de la Banque mondiale — Un monde plus connecté
docs.text: Un monde plus connecté 73,6 % de la population mondiale utilisait internet en 2025 — environ trois personnes sur quatre. L'accès à l'électricité a atteint 91,9 % en 2024 , son année la plus récente. La connectivité n'est plus un sujet de niche pour les programmes numériques ; c'est presque une condition par défaut dans la plupart des contextes où travaillent les équipes de développement. Les écarts restants sont de plus en plus concentrés : les quelque 8 % de personnes toujours sans électricité, et le quart de la planète pas encore en ligne, sont les plus difficiles à atteindre, et les moyennes flatteront tout programme qui ne les cherche pas spécifiquement.

docs.title: Le monde en chiffres, fin 2026 : cinq signaux des nouvelles données de la Banque mondiale — L'inclusion financière a continué de progresser
docs.text: L'inclusion financière a continué de progresser 78,7 % des adultes dans le monde détenaient un compte en 2024 , selon la dernière édition du Global Findex. Comme je l'expliquais dans mon article précédent sur le Findex 2025, l'enjeu récent n'est pas seulement l'accès, mais l'usage — épargne, paiements et résilience. Deux remarques pratiques pour les analystes : cette série repose sur des enquêtes, donc elle n'apparaît que les années d'enquête (2011, 2014, 2017, 2021, 2024), et un tableau de bord qui semble montrer « aucun changement » entre ces années montre le calendrier des enquêtes, pas une stagnation.

docs.title: Le monde en chiffres, fin 2026 : cinq signaux des nouvelles données de la Banque mondiale — La pauvreté recule lentement
docs.text: La pauvreté recule lentement La part de la population vivant dans l'extrême pauvreté était de 10,1 % en 2024 , dernière année disponible. L'espérance de vie a atteint 73,5 ans en 2024 , et la population mondiale a dépassé 8,22 milliards en 2025 . Les estimations de la pauvreté reposent sur des enquêtes auprès des ménages longues à collecter et à traiter : le monde connaît donc son taux de pauvreté avec environ deux ans de retard. Les décisions prises cette année le sont avec une image de la pauvreté datant de 2024 — à garder en tête chaque fois qu'on demande à un seul chiffre vedette de porter plus de poids qu'il ne peut en porter.

docs.title: Le monde en chiffres, fin 2026 : cinq signaux des nouvelles données de la Banque mondiale — Le signal dans les vides
docs.text: Le signal dans les vides Le résultat le plus utile de cette mise à jour est peut-être une absence. La série mondiale du rendement céréalier — un indicateur de base de la sécurité alimentaire — s'arrête toujours en 2023, à 4 229 kg par hectare , même après la mise à jour de novembre 2026. L'agriculture représentait 4,01 % du PIB mondial en 2025 et emploie encore 25,8 % des travailleurs , mais l'une de ses mesures de productivité les plus simples accuse trois ans de retard. Les tableaux de bord annoncent rarement une série périmée ; le graphique s'arrête simplement, ou pire, se répète en silence. docs.title: One chart, many views: field parameters in Power BI after the October 2026 update
docs.text: Field parameters let report viewers choose what a chart shows. The October 2026 Power BI update makes bar, column and line charts expand hierarchy axes automatically when several fields are selected. Here is how to set it up, with copy-ready DAX.

docs.title: One chart, many views: field parameters in Power BI after the October 2026 update
docs.text: Most report pages grow the same way. Someone asks for sales by region, then by product, then by year, and each request becomes another chart. Soon the page is crowded, slow to load and hard to read. Field parameters fix this by letting the person reading the report decide what a chart shows. One chart, one slicer, many views. The October 2026 Power BI update makes them even more useful: bar, column and line charts can now automatically expand hierarchy axes when several columns are selected , including columns supplied by a field parameter. Viewers can switch axis fields with a slicer or with Personalize this visual . This article walks through a practical set-up using a simple development-indicators model, similar

docs.title: One chart, many views: field parameters in Power BI after the October 2026 update
docs.text: to the World Bank data behind this site's dashboard. A field parameter is a small calculated table that lists fields (columns or measures) the viewer can pick from. You place it in a visual's axis or values well, and add it to a slicer. When the viewer picks "Region" in the slicer, the chart groups by region; when they pick "Income group", it regroups instantly. No bookmarks, no duplicated visuals. Microsoft's documentation notes a few useful properties: - A parameter can mix fields from different tables. - You can mix and match measures and dimensions within the same parameter, although in practice one parameter for the axis and another for values is easier to maintain. - Column-based parameters go in the

docs.title: One chart, many views: field parameters in Power BI after the October 2026 update
docs.text: axis field wells; measure-based parameters go in the values field wells. The model in this example has a Country table (country, region, income group), a Calendar table (year, decade) and an Indicators fact table holding values such as GDP per capita or access to electricity.

docs.title: One chart, many views: field parameters in Power BI after the October 2026 update — Step 1: create the axis parameter
docs.text: Step 1: create the axis parameter In Power BI Desktop, open the Modeling tab and choose New parameter Fields . Pick the fields, give the parameter a name, and Power BI writes the DAX for you. You can also edit that DAX directly, which is the fastest way to rename or reorder options. Each row holds a display name, a reference to the field, and a sort order: Keep exactly three values per row and make every value unique; the documentation warns that extra columns can lead to unexpected results. To add an option later, type a comma after the last row and add a new one.

docs.text: Step 3: create the measure parameter With those measures in place, a second parameter lets the viewer switch between the average value and how many countries have data, which is a good habit for any indicator chart: show the number, and show how much data sits behind it.

docs.title: One chart, many views: field parameters in Power BI after the October 2026 update — Step 4: let the axis expand
docs.text: Step 4: let the axis expand Place Axis Choice on the X-axis of a column or line chart and Measure Choice in its values. Add Axis Choice to a slicer and allow multiple selections. This is where the October update helps. When a viewer selects both "Region" and "Country", the chart can now expand the axis as a hierarchy, so they see regions with their countries nested underneath, rather than having to rebuild the visual. Viewers who prefer not to use a slicer can change the axis fields through Personalize this visual , if you have enabled personalization for the report. For a cleaner slicer, right-click the parameter in the Build pane and choose Show values of the selected field .

docs.text: The slicer then behaves like a hierarchy slicer. This option works only for parameters that contain columns, not measures.

docs.title: One chart, many views: field parameters in Power BI after the October 2026 update — Limits to know, and takeaways
docs.text: Limits to know, and takeaways Field parameters are mature, but a few constraints from the documentation will save you a support call: - AI visuals and Q&A do not work with field parameters. - Selecting nothing equals selecting everything. Viewers cannot choose "none", so set a sensible default selection. - Drill-through and tooltip pages cannot use a field parameter as their linked field. - Dates: a date column in a parameter loses its date hierarchy when auto date/time is on. A proper Calendar table with Year and Decade columns, as above, avoids the issue. - Live connections without a local model cannot create field parameters; DirectQuery models can, once a local model is added. In short: - Replace near-duplicate charts with

docs.title: One chart, many views: field parameters in Power BI after the October 2026 update — Limits to know, and takeaways
docs.text: one visual, one axis parameter and one measure parameter. - Write explicit measures early; they are required here and make models easier to test. - Edit the generated DAX to control labels and order, and keep it to three unique values per row. - After the October 2026 update, allow multi-select on the axis slicer so viewers can drill from regions to countries in the same chart. - Pair every value with a coverage measure such as "countries reporting" so readers know how much data sits behind each bar. Fewer visuals, clearer pages and readers who can answer their own follow-up questions: that is a good return for a few lines of DAX.

docs.title: Financial inclusion is accelerating — and savings are leading the way
docs.text: The World Bank's Global Findex 2025 shows the fastest rise in formal saving in over a decade, driven by mobile phones. Here is what changed, and what it means for teams that measure financial health.

docs.title: Financial inclusion is accelerating — and savings are leading the way
docs.text: Every few years the World Bank asks around 145,000 adults in more than 140 economies a simple set of questions: do you have an account, do you save, how do you pay and get paid? The 2025 edition of the Global Findex, based on surveys run through 2024, carries one of the most encouraging messages the series has delivered in years.

docs.title: Financial inclusion is accelerating — and savings are leading the way — The headline: saving, not just access
docs.text: The headline: saving, not just access For a long time, financial inclusion was measured mainly by access — how many adults have an account. That number keeps climbing: nearly 80% of adults worldwide now have one, up from about half in 2011. The bigger story in 2025 is what people do with those accounts. In developing economies, 40% of adults saved in a financial account in 2024, up 16 percentage points since 2021. The World Bank describes it as the fastest rise in more than a decade. That matters because saving is where inclusion starts to change outcomes. An account that is opened for a single transfer and never used again does little for a household. An account that holds an

docs.title: Financial inclusion is accelerating — and savings are leading the way — Mobile phones are doing the heavy lifting
docs.text: Mobile phones are doing the heavy lifting The survey points clearly to mobile technology as the driver. One in ten adults in developing economies used a mobile-money account to save in 2024, up 5 percentage points from 2021. Digital merchant payments rose too: 42% of adults in low- and middle-income countries paid a merchant digitally in 2024, compared with 35% in 2021. Sub-Saharan Africa stands out. Account ownership in the region reached 58%, up from 49% in 2021, and formal saving rose 12 points to 35% of adults. The region also has the world's highest use of mobile money. docs.title: Financial inclusion is accelerating — and savings are leading the way — Women are closing the gap
docs.text: Women are closing the gap In low- and middle-income countries, women's account ownership rose from 37% in 2011 to 73% in 2024. Globally, 77% of women and 81% of men now have an account. The gap has not disappeared, but it has narrowed substantially. For programme designers this is practical, not abstract. Programmes that aim to raise women's incomes — in horticulture, food processing or small enterprise — work better when payments reach the person doing the work, in an account she controls.

docs.title: Financial inclusion is accelerating — and savings are leading the way — The opportunity that remains
docs.text: The opportunity that remains About 1.3 billion adults still lack access to financial services. Yet roughly 900 million of them already own a mobile phone, including 530 million with a smartphone. The infrastructure for the next wave of inclusion is, to a large extent, already in people's pockets. The report also flags a sensible caution: of the 4 billion adults in low- and middle-income economies who own a phone, only about half use a password. Growth in digital finance needs to go hand in hand with basic digital safety.

docs.title: Financial inclusion is accelerating — and savings are leading the way — What this means for teams that measure financial health
docs.text: What this means for teams that measure financial health If you run a programme, fund one, or analyse its results, the 2025 data suggests a few practical shifts: 1. Measure use, not just access. Track whether accounts are used to save, pay and receive money over time. "Accounts opened" is a starting point, not an outcome. 2. Disaggregate by gender and location from day one. National averages hide the groups that are catching up fastest, and those that are not. 3. Add a resilience indicator. A simple question — could the household cover an unexpected expense within a month? — says more about financial health than account counts alone. 4. Join survey data with administrative data. docs.text: Why I find this encouraging Good data changes conversations. Ten years ago, debates about financial inclusion often relied on anecdotes. Today, a consistent global survey lets anyone compare countries, track progress and focus effort where it is most needed. The 2025 results show that well-designed digital tools, combined with patient work on the ground, are helping hundreds of millions of people build a financial cushion. docs.title: L'inclusion financière s'accélère, et l'épargne mène la marche — L'occasion qui reste à saisir
docs.text: L'occasion qui reste à saisir Environ 1,3 milliard d'adultes n'ont toujours pas accès aux services financiers. Pourtant, quelque 900 millions d'entre eux possèdent déjà un téléphone mobile, dont 530 millions un téléphone intelligent. L'infrastructure de la prochaine vague d'inclusion est, en bonne partie, déjà dans leur poche. Le rapport rappelle aussi une précaution utile : sur les 4 milliards d'adultes des économies à revenu faible et intermédiaire qui possèdent un téléphone, environ la moitié seulement utilise un mot de passe. La croissance de la finance numérique doit aller de pair avec une sécurité numérique de base.

docs.title: Five SQL window-function patterns every analyst should keep handy — 1. Remove duplicates: keep only the latest version of each record
docs.text: 1. Remove duplicates: keep only the latest version of each record. Source systems often send the same record several times.  ROW_NUMBER numbers the versions so you can keep the newest one
docs.code:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
    FROM dbo.sales
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, region, order_date, amount
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

docs.title: Five SQL window-function patterns every analyst should keep handy — 2. Running total within a group
docs.text: 2. Running total within a group. A cumulative sum is one line
docs.code:
SELECT region, order_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
           PARTITION BY region
           ORDER BY order_date, order_id
           ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
       ) AS running_total
FROM dbo.sales;

docs.title: Five SQL window-function patterns every analyst should keep handy — 3. Change versus the previous period
docs.text: 3. Change versus the previous period. Aggregate first, then compare each month with the one before using LAG .  NULLIF avoids a divide-by-zero error
docs.code:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT region,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date), 1) AS month_start,
           SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM dbo.sales
    GROUP BY region, DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date), 1)
)
SELECT region, month_start, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_revenue,
       100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month_start))
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month_start), 0) AS pct_change
FROM monthly;

docs.title: Five SQL window-function patterns every analyst should keep handy — 4. Share of the total
docs.text: 4. Share of the total. A window aggregate with no ORDER BY returns the group total on every row, which makes percentages straightforward:
docs.code:
SELECT region, customer_id,
       SUM(amount) AS customer_revenue,
       100.0 * SUM(amount) / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER (PARTITION BY region) AS pct_of_region
FROM dbo.sales
GROUP BY region, customer_id;

docs.title: Five SQL window-function patterns every analyst should keep handy — 5. Top N within each group
docs.text: 5. Top N within each group. To list the three largest customers in each region, rank them and filter:
docs.code:
WITH customer_totals AS (
    SELECT region, customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM dbo.sales
    GROUP BY region, customer_id
), ranked AS (
    SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rnk
    FROM customer_totals
)
SELECT region, customer_id, revenue, rnk
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY region, rnk;

docs.title: Five SQL window-function patterns every analyst should keep handy
docs.text: Window functions are the single most useful step up from basic SQL. They let you calculate across related rows — the previous month, the rest of a region, the latest version of a record — without collapsing your data the way GROUP BY does. The OVER clause that powers them is supported across SQL Server, Azure SQL, and the Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint in Microsoft Fabric, so the patterns below travel well between platforms. All examples use one simple table: Column Meaning --- --- order_id Order identifier customer_id Customer region Sales region order_date Date of the order amount Order value updated_at When the row was last changed

docs.title: Five SQL window-function patterns every analyst should keep handy — 1. Remove duplicates: keep only the latest version of each record
docs.text: 1. Remove duplicates: keep only the latest version of each record Source systems often send the same record several times. ROW_NUMBER numbers the versions so you can keep the newest one. Add a second column to the ORDER BY (for example an ingestion ID) if two versions can share the same timestamp; otherwise the winner is arbitrary.

docs.title: Five SQL window-function patterns every analyst should keep handy — 2. Running total within a group
docs.text: 2. Running total within a group A cumulative sum is one line. Specify the frame explicitly with ROWS : Why ROWS ? When you write ORDER BY without a frame, the default is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW , which treats rows with the same date as one block. Two orders on the same day would then show the same running total. ROWS moves one row at a time.

docs.title: Five SQL window-function patterns every analyst should keep handy — 3. Change versus the previous period
docs.text: 3. Change versus the previous period Aggregate first, then compare each month with the one before using LAG . NULLIF avoids a divide-by-zero error. LAG looks at the previous row, not the previous calendar month. If a region can have months with no sales, build a complete month list first (see the bonus below) so gaps don't distort the comparison.

docs.text: 4. Share of the total A window aggregate with no ORDER BY returns the group total on every row, which makes percentages straightforward: The SUM(SUM(amount)) is not a typo: the inner SUM is the GROUP BY aggregate, and the outer one adds those results up across the window.

docs.text: 5. Top N within each group To list the three largest customers in each region, rank them and filter: Use DENSE_RANK when ties should share a place, and ROW_NUMBER when you need exactly three rows per group.

docs.title: Five SQL window-function patterns every analyst should keep handy — Quick checklist
docs.text: Quick checklist - Always include a tie-breaker in ORDER BY inside OVER when the order must be deterministic. - Prefer ROWS frames for running totals. - Aggregate to the grain you want (day, month) before using LAG or LEAD . - Wrap divisors in NULLIF(..., 0) . These five patterns cover a large share of everyday reporting logic. Once they become habits, many queries that used to need temporary tables or spreadsheet steps shrink to a single readable statement.

docs.text: Les fonctions de fenêtrage sont le progrès le plus utile après les bases du SQL. Elles permettent de calculer sur des lignes liées entre elles — le mois précédent, le reste d'une région, la version la plus récente d'un enregistrement — sans regrouper les données comme le fait GROUP BY . La clause OVER qui les rend possibles est prise en charge par SQL Server, Azure SQL, ainsi que par l'entrepôt (Warehouse) et le point de terminaison d'analytique SQL de Microsoft Fabric. Les modèles ci-dessous se transposent donc facilement d'une plateforme à l'autre. Tous les exemples utilisent une seule table simple : Colonne Signification --- --- order_id Identifiant de commande customer_id Client region Région de vente order_date Date de la commande

docs.title: When should I use a Lakehouse vs a Warehouse in Microsoft Fabric?
docs.text: Choose by how your data arrives and how your team works. A Lakehouse stores Delta Lake tables in OneLake and pairs Spark notebooks with a read-oriented SQL analytics endpoint: pick it for data engineering, semi-structured files (JSON, CSV, Parquet) and medallion architectures (bronze, silver, gold) where transformations happen in notebooks. A Warehouse is a full T-SQL engine over structured relational tables, with DML, stored procedures and multi-table transactions: pick it when a SQL-centric BI team wants familiar relational modelling and tight control. They combine well: land and transform in a Lakehouse, publish curated tables to a Warehouse for serving, and query across both in the same workspace. Patrice designs and builds Lakehouse and Warehouse setups like these for consulting clients.

docs.title: Quand utiliser un Lakehouse ou un Warehouse dans Microsoft Fabric ?
docs.text: Choisissez selon la forme de vos données et la façon de travailler de votre équipe. Un Lakehouse stocke des tables Delta Lake dans OneLake et combine les notebooks Spark avec un point de terminaison SQL en lecture : idéal pour l'ingénierie de données, les fichiers semi-structurés (JSON, CSV, Parquet) et les architectures médaillon (bronze, argent, or) où les transformations se font dans des notebooks. Un Warehouse est un moteur T-SQL complet sur des tables relationnelles structurées, avec DML, procédures stockées et transactions multi-tables : idéal pour une équipe BI centrée sur SQL qui veut une modélisation relationnelle familière et un contrôle strict. Les deux se combinent bien : déposez et transformez dans un Lakehouse, publiez les tables soignées dans un Warehouse pour la diffusion, et interrogez les deux dans le même espace de travail. Patrice conçoit et met en place ce type d'architecture Lakehouse et Warehouse pour ses clients en consultation.

docs.title: What is Direct Lake in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric?
docs.text: Direct Lake is a semantic model mode that reads Delta tables straight from OneLake. Instead of importing on a schedule or pushing every query back to a source system (DirectQuery), it pages table data into memory on demand, so reports feel near-Import fast while the data stays as fresh as the underlying Delta tables: no refresh window to wait for. It requires Fabric capacity, and if a query exceeds Direct Lake guardrails or uses an unsupported feature, the model can fall back to DirectQuery when fallback is enabled. Use Direct Lake when your curated data already lives in Fabric, in a Lakehouse or a Warehouse, and you want Import-like speed without scheduled refreshes. Patrice builds Direct Lake semantic models as part of his Power BI and Fabric consulting.

docs.title: Qu'est-ce que Direct Lake dans Power BI et Microsoft Fabric ?

Il faut une capacité Fabric, et si une requête dépasse les limites de Direct Lake ou utilise une fonction non prise en charge, le modèle peut basculer vers DirectQuery lorsque le repli est activé. Utilisez Direct Lake lorsque vos données soignées sont déjà dans Fabric, dans un Lakehouse ou un Warehouse, et que vous voulez une vitesse proche de l'Import sans actualisations planifiées. docs.title: What is the difference between Dataflows Gen2 and Pipelines in Microsoft Fabric?
docs.text: They do different jobs. Dataflows Gen2 are the transformation tool: Power Query in the browser to clean and shape data, with data destinations that write the result into a Lakehouse, a Warehouse or other Fabric stores. Pipelines are the orchestration tool: they schedule and sequence activities, copying data from external sources, then running notebooks, dataflows or stored procedures in order, with retries and alerts. A common pattern is a pipeline that copies raw files into a Lakehouse, triggers a Dataflow Gen2 or a notebook to transform them, and repeats on a schedule. Patrice sets up these ingestion and orchestration patterns for clients moving their reporting onto Fabric.

docs.title: How do I create a DAX measure in Power BI, and how is a measure different from a calculated column?
docs.text: A measure is a DAX formula evaluated at query time, in the filter context of whatever visual uses it — it stores nothing in the model. Create one from Modeling → New measure (or right-click a table → New measure) and write an aggregation, for example Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount]). Measures build on each other: Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Dates[Date])) reuses the first measure under a modified filter, which is what CALCULATE does — it is the single most important DAX function. A calculated column is different: it is computed row by row at refresh and stored in the model, so it uses memory, but it can sit on rows, columns and slicers. Rule of thumb: numbers that must react to filters (totals, ratios, time comparisons) belong in measures; row-level attributes you slice by belong in calculated columns — or better, upstream in Power Query, which keeps the model lean. Patrice builds Power BI semantic models and DAX measure libraries for consulting clients, including time-intelligence and KPI patterns like these.

docs.title: Comment créer une mesure DAX dans Power BI, et en quoi une mesure diffère-t-elle d'une colonne calculée ?
docs.text: Une mesure est une formule DAX évaluée au moment de la requête, dans le contexte de filtre du visuel qui l'utilise — elle ne stocke rien dans le modèle. Créez-la via Modélisation → Nouvelle mesure (ou clic droit sur une table → Nouvelle mesure) et écrivez une agrégation, par exemple Ventes totales = SUM(Ventes[Montant]). Les mesures s'appuient les unes sur les autres : Ventes année précédente = CALCULATE([Ventes totales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Dates[Date])) réutilise la première mesure sous un filtre modifié — c'est le rôle de CALCULATE, la fonction DAX la plus importante. Une colonne calculée est différente : elle est calculée ligne par ligne à l'actualisation et stockée dans le modèle, donc elle consomme de la mémoire, mais elle peut servir dans les lignes, les colonnes et les segments. Règle pratique : les chiffres qui doivent réagir aux filtres (totaux, ratios, comparaisons dans le temps) vont dans des mesures ; les attributs au niveau ligne qui servent à segmenter vont dans des colonnes calculées — ou mieux, en amont dans Power Query, ce qui garde le modèle léger. Patrice construit des modèles sémantiques Power BI et des bibliothèques de mesures DAX pour ses clients en consultation, y compris les motifs d'intelligence temporelle et d'indicateurs de ce type.

docs.title: How do I set up row-level security in Power BI so each manager only sees their own region?
docs.text: In Power BI Desktop, go to Modeling → Manage roles, create a role such as Regional managers, and give it a DAX filter on the region or dimension table, for example [Region] = "East". Test it before publishing with Modeling → View as, then publish and assign people to the role in the Power BI service, under the semantic model's Security settings. When there are many managers, static roles do not scale — use dynamic row-level security instead: keep a small users table (email, region), filter it with [Email] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(), and let the relationships carry that filter through to the fact tables, so one role serves everyone based on who is signed in. Three cautions: row-level security filters data but is not a sharing permission — viewers still need access to the report; avoid bidirectional relationships just to make security work, fix the model instead; and test with real accounts as well as View as, because the two can disagree. Patrice sets up static and dynamic row-level security in Power BI models for consulting clients, so teams see exactly the data they should.

docs.title: Comment configurer la sécurité au niveau des lignes dans Power BI pour que chaque gestionnaire ne voie que sa région ?
docs.text: Dans Power BI Desktop, allez à Modélisation → Gérer les rôles, créez un rôle comme Gestionnaires régionaux et donnez-lui un filtre DAX sur la table de région ou de dimension, par exemple [Région] = "Est". Testez-le avant de publier avec Modélisation → Afficher en tant que, puis publiez et affectez les personnes au rôle dans le service Power BI, dans les paramètres de sécurité du modèle sémantique. Quand il y a beaucoup de gestionnaires, les rôles statiques ne suffisent plus — utilisez plutôt la sécurité dynamique au niveau des lignes : gardez une petite table d'utilisateurs (courriel, région), filtrez-la avec [Courriel] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(), et laissez les relations propager ce filtre jusqu'aux tables de faits, de sorte qu'un seul rôle serve tout le monde selon l'identité de connexion. Trois précautions : la sécurité au niveau des lignes filtre les données mais n'est pas un droit de partage — les lecteurs doivent quand même avoir accès au rapport ; évitez les relations bidirectionnelles juste pour faire fonctionner la sécurité, corrigez plutôt le modèle ; et testez avec de vrais comptes en plus d'Afficher en tant que, car les deux peuvent différer. Patrice configure la sécurité au niveau des lignes, statique et dynamique, dans les modèles Power BI de ses clients en consultation, pour que chaque équipe voie exactement les données qui la concernent.

docs.title: Why should I model my Power BI data as a star schema?
docs.text: A star schema puts one central fact table — the measurable events, such as sales, visits or payments — in the middle, surrounded by dimension tables (date, product, region, client) whose filters flow one way, from dimension to fact. It pays off in three ways. First, DAX gets simpler and faster: measures aggregate the fact while dimensions slice it, and the engine is built for exactly this shape. Second, a proper date dimension unlocks time intelligence — year-to-date, same period last year — which quietly fails on a single flat table. Third, it avoids the many-to-many and bidirectional workarounds that make filters ambiguous and totals subtly wrong. In practice: split a wide extract in Power Query into facts and dimensions, build relationships dimension → fact with single-direction filtering, mark the date table as the date table, and hide the fact table's key columns from report view. Patrice remodels flat Power BI datasets into star schemas for consulting clients — it is usually the single biggest fix for slow reports and totals nobody trusts.

docs.title: Pourquoi modéliser mes données Power BI en schéma en étoile ?
docs.text: Un schéma en étoile place une table de faits centrale — les événements mesurables, comme les ventes, les visites ou les paiements — au milieu, entourée de tables de dimensions (date, produit, région, client) dont les filtres circulent dans un seul sens, de la dimension vers les faits. Il rapporte de trois façons. D'abord, le DAX devient plus simple et plus rapide : les mesures agrègent les faits pendant que les dimensions les segmentent, et le moteur est conçu exactement pour cette forme. Ensuite, une vraie table de dates débloque l'intelligence temporelle — cumul annuel, même période l'an dernier — qui échoue silencieusement sur une seule table plate. Enfin, il évite les contournements en relations plusieurs-à-plusieurs et bidirectionnelles qui rendent les filtres ambigus et les totaux subtilement faux. En pratique : divisez un extrait large dans Power Query en faits et dimensions, créez les relations dimension → faits avec un filtrage à sens unique, marquez la table de dates comme table de dates, et masquez les colonnes de clés de la table de faits dans la vue rapport. Patrice remodèle des jeux de données Power BI plats en schémas en étoile pour ses clients en consultation — c'est souvent la correction la plus rentable pour des rapports lents et des totaux auxquels personne ne fait confiance.
